01.event: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and Levite.
01.turn: He did not know the answer and went to ask Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha.
01.outcome: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha gave him the order of precedence for Torah readers.
01.summary: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question: after the priest and the Levite, who is called to read the Torah? He did not know, so he went and asked Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, who told him the order: scholars appointed as community leaders, then scholars fit to be appointed, then sons of such leaders, then synagogue heads and everyone else.
01.missing: The passage segment alone breaks off mid-question; the rest of the episode is in the following context segment, and it is mainly a legal answer.

02.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down to let his mother step on him getting into and out of bed, and boasted of it in the study hall.
02.turn: The sages told him he had not reached even half the honor due her.
02.outcome: He was humbled with the example of a mother who throws a purse into the sea without being shamed by her son.
02.summary: Rabbi Tarfon honored his mother by bending down so she could climb onto him to get into and out of bed. He came and praised himself for this in the study hall. The sages answered that he had not reached even half of the honor due to her: had she ever thrown his purse into the sea before his eyes without his embarrassing her?

03.actor: a man's daughter and the orphan heirs
03.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter, but the heirs divided the estate without giving her one.
03.turn: Rav Yosef thought the case matched the mishna where each heir can deflect the claim, but Abaye showed the tree is a shared obligation.
03.outcome: Abaye ruled they must give her a palm tree and redivide the estate from the start.
03.summary: A man said in his will that his daughter should get a palm tree. His sons divided the estate and gave her nothing. Rav Yosef thought each brother could claim the tree was in someone else's share, as in the mishna, but Abaye disagreed: here the obligation rests on all of them. His remedy: give her a palm tree and divide the inheritance again from the beginning.

04.event: The two schools disputed for two and a half years whether it would have been better for man not to have been created.
04.outcome: They concluded it would have been better not to be created, but now that man exists he should examine his deeds.
04.summary: For two and a half years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argued over whether humanity would have been better off never created. In the end they counted votes and decided it would have been better not to be created; but since we are here, a person should examine his deeds.
04.missing: The dispute itself is only a stated opinion; there is little narrative beyond the duration and the vote.

05.event: A ritual bath in Yavne presumed full was measured and found deficient, and Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva disputed whether purifications done in it were valid.
05.turn: Rabbi Akiva produced an analysis showing the bath resembles a blemished priest, not one of flawed lineage.
05.outcome: Rabbi Tarfon conceded, saying anyone who separates from Akiva separates from life.
05.summary: A reservoir in Yavne thought to hold enough water for a ritual bath was measured and found short. Rabbi Tarfon ruled that the purifications done in it stood, while Rabbi Akiva ruled them void, and they traded arguments and parables about priests discovered to be disqualified. Rabbi Akiva then showed why the bath is like a blemished priest, whose service is invalid. Rabbi Tarfon accepted it and told him that whoever parts from him parts from life.

06.event: Ravin went as agent to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her to himself.
06.turn: Her family refused to give her to the son, and Ravin feared someone else would betroth her while he went to report back.
06.summary: Ravin the Pious went to betroth a woman on his son's behalf but ended up betrothing her to himself. Her family would not give her to his son, only to him. Rather than first telling his son, he acted at once, fearing that in the meantime another man would come and betroth her.

07.event: Ravina examined a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia during the lifetime of his teacher Rav Ashi.
07.turn: Rav Ashi challenged him, and Ravina cited Rav Hamnuna's precedent; when Rav Ashi disputed the tradition, Ravina reconciled both versions.
07.outcome: Ravina defended himself as Rav Ashi's disciple-colleague, permitted to rule in another town.
07.summary: Ravina checked a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia while his teacher Rav Ashi was alive, and Rav Ashi asked why he had done it. Ravina pointed to Rav Hamnuna, who ruled in another town during his teacher Rav Hisda's life. Rav Ashi replied that the tradition was that Hamnuna did not rule; Ravina answered that both traditions were true, since Hamnuna was Rav Hisda's disciple-colleague, and so was Ravina to Rav Ashi.

09.actor: Rabbi Banai and the orphan daughters
09.event: Rabbi Banai held movable property belonging to orphans, and the daughters came before Shmuel.
09.outcome: Shmuel told Rabbi Banai to go and support the daughters from it.
09.summary: Rabbi Banai, brother of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, was holding movable property that belonged to some orphans. The orphan daughters brought the matter to Shmuel, who told Rabbi Banai to go and provide for them from it.
09.missing: It is cited as a precedent; there is no real turn, and the purpose of the payment is left for the legal discussion.

11.event: A case about establishing priestly status came before Rabbi Yohanan, and Reish Lakish again demanded proof from the threshing floor.
11.turn: Rabbi Yohanan gave the same retort Rabbi Elazar had given earlier, revealing that Elazar had been quoting him.
11.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name.
11.summary: Earlier, when Reish Lakish insisted a man's priesthood be proven by receiving teruma at the threshing floor, Rabbi Elazar objected: if there is no threshing floor, does priesthood cease? Later, sitting before Rabbi Yohanan, the same kind of case arose, Reish Lakish asked the same question, and Rabbi Yohanan answered with the very same words. Reish Lakish looked harshly at Rabbi Elazar and said: you heard this from the blacksmith's son and did not tell us in his name?

13.event: Bar Shatya, who was intermittently insane, sold property, and two pairs of witnesses contradicted each other about his state at the sale.
13.turn: Rav Ashi held that the two testimonies cancel out.
13.outcome: The land stayed in Bar Shatya's possession.
13.summary: A man called Bar Shatya, who sometimes went insane, sold some property. Two witnesses said he sold it while sane; two others said he was insane at the time. Rav Ashi ruled that the testimonies cancel each other, so the land remained in Bar Shatya's hands.

14.event: A man grabbed coins from someone else and threw them to a woman washing her feet, declaring her betrothed to him.
14.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal void, since the coins were stolen and the owner had not given up on them.
14.summary: A woman was washing her feet in a basin of water when a man snatched some coins from another person, tossed them to her, and said, 'You are betrothed to me.' The case came to Rava, who ruled that no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that a robbery victim gives up hope, so the coins were not the man's and the betrothal had no effect.

15.actor: Rabbi Abbahu and his attendant Rabbi Nahum
15.event: While walking leaning on Rabbi Nahum's shoulder, Rabbi Abbahu answered his attendant's questions about when the halakha follows an unattributed mishna.
15.turn: Rabbi Nahum challenged him with a mishna on combs whose unattributed ruling is not followed.
15.outcome: He was told that mishna is an exception, since Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish said it is not an authoritative mishna.
15.summary: Rabbi Abbahu used to walk leaning on the shoulder of his attendant Rabbi Nahum, who would gather rulings from him on the way. Nahum asked a series of questions on how to rule when a mishna or baraita gives an unattributed opinion alongside a dispute, and Abbahu answered each. When Nahum challenged him with a mishna about flax and wool combs that is not followed, he was told that mishna is an exception, declared non-authoritative by Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish.
15.missing: Beyond the walking frame, this is a legal question-and-answer with no event; the translation also names Rabbi Hiyya as respondent in the later part, which is unclear.

16.event: A woman gave birth twelve months after her husband went overseas.
16.outcome: Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child legitimate, presuming a delayed pregnancy.
16.summary: A woman's husband went overseas, and she gave birth twelve months after he left. Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child legitimate, treating the husband as the father on the view that a pregnancy can be delayed.
16.missing: The case is only cited as a precedent; there is no development beyond the ruling.

17.event: Ameimar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza.
17.turn: Rav Ashi challenged him, noting that three schools did not teach the ruling he relied on.
17.outcome: Ameimar did not accept the objection, because he had heard the ruling directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.
17.summary: Ameimar allowed Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza, a place of doubtful lineage. Rav Ashi questioned him: the schools of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid did not teach the ruling that all lands are presumed of good lineage. Ameimar stood by his decision, since he had heard it directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.

18.event: Rabbi Tavla visited Mehoza and saw a bolt hanging from the side of a door.
18.outcome: He said nothing to the people there.
18.summary: Rabbi Tavla came to Mehoza and saw a door bolt hanging from the side of a doorway, not tied to the door. He said nothing against it; the Gemara explains it was the kind of bolt lifted by its rope.
18.missing: It is a brief observation cited as evidence; there is no turn or development.

19.event: Yehuda bar Mareimar escorted Rav Pappa to the house of Abba of Sura for his son's marriage contract but did not want to enter.
19.turn: Pressed to enter, he sat silent; Abba of Sura took the silence for anger and wrote all his property into the dowry.
19.outcome: Yehuda said he did not want this, but told Abba not to retract and make himself a man who goes back on his word.
19.summary: Rav Pappa went to have the marriage contract written for his son, who was marrying into the family of Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to accompany him but would not go inside. Yehuda explained that his mere presence would pressure the father into a larger dowry; Rav Pappa made him enter anyway. Yehuda sat in silence, and Abba of Sura, thinking he was angry, signed over everything he owned as a dowry. When Yehuda said he had not wanted that, Abba offered to retract, but Yehuda told him not to become a man who goes back on his word.

20.event: An incident arose involving loss caused by voiding a sold promissory note.
20.turn: Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to issue an unequivocal ruling.
20.outcome: Rav Ashi had the full value of the note collected, as for damaging a beam meant for a sculpture.
20.summary: A case came up in which a creditor forgave a loan after selling the note, causing loss to the buyer. Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to rule decisively, and Rav Ashi made the creditor pay the full value of the note.
20.missing: The facts of the incident are given only by reference to the preceding legal discussion; no parties or details are named.
